title: The misery of being human (I.22)
hookLine: every life has sorrow; the wise make peace with it
tomorrow: what would change if tonight were the last time?

lines: SEE HOW WELL THAT PERSON LIVES.
NOT EVEN A KING OR A POPE.
cards: Scroll long enough and everyone else seems fine. The beach trip, the new car, the couple laughing at a dinner that looks warm through the screen. The Imitation had a version of this, long before screens.
Some people, it says, look at someone else and sigh: see how well that person lives, how rich, how great, how powerful. Then it answers with a question. Who has everything just as they want it?
Not me, not you, not anyone on earth. Not even, it adds, a king or a pope.

teach.b: Chapter twenty-two of book one has a title that sounds bleak: the misery of being human. It isn't there to darken anyone's day. It's clearing away a false hope, that somebody, somewhere, has a life without sorrow.
And notice where it looks for proof. Not in disasters, or in some tragic story. In the body.
Eating, drinking, sleeping, waking, working, resting: the plain needs of a body, which the chapter says a devout person feels as a weight. Hunger at eleven. The yawn at three in the afternoon.
The knee that aches when it rains. That's the misery the book means, and everyone with a body shares it. Then it borrows a psalm's prayer.
In the Douay-Rheims: "deliver me from my necessities." Then comes the turn, and it's a sharp one.
The chapter asks who is actually better off, and it doesn't say the rich one or the healthy one. It says the one who is able to suffer something for God.
Having plenty of passing things isn't what makes a person happy, it says; a modest amount is enough. So the envy at the screen loses its footing. The person who looks fine gets hungry at eleven too.
Peace doesn't come from finding the life without limits.
It comes from turning to God inside the limits everyone shares.

how: Catholics speak of 'offering up' sufferings and accepting limits as part of following Christ, and the Imitation's chapters on human misery are read in spiritual reading and on retreats.

games.q: what does “the misery of being human” mean?
o: every life has trouble; peace comes in turning to God
suffering proves that someone did something wrong
human beings are worthless and should feel ashamed

games.q: the honest chapter — tap the pairs.
p: the one who can suffer for God

s: the Imitation says some lucky people live without trouble
who has everything as they want it? not anyone on earth, it says, not even a king or a pope.
the chapter names eating and sleeping among the body's burdens
eating, drinking, sleeping, waking, working, resting: the plain needs everyone shares.
the misery of being human means life is pointless
the chapter turns to God within the limits, and calls the one who can suffer something for God better off.

games.q: a coworker always seems cheerful and lucky, and you catch yourself resenting it. by chapter twenty-two, what's most likely true?
o: they carry trouble too; nobody has everything as they wish.
they really have it easy, so the resentment is fair.
they're faking it, so they deserve less credit.
games.why: the chapter says no one on earth, not even a king or a pope, has everything as they want it. the envy loses its footing.

practice: Sit and press both feet into the floor. Notice one thing your body needs right now, water, rest, food, a stretch, and don't fix it yet; just feel it as a limit everyone carries, the well-known and the unknown alike.
If you pray, you can borrow the psalm: deliver me from my necessities.

wordCard.voice: The misery of being human. The Imitation's honest line: every life carries trouble, even the one that looks perfect from outside.

carryVoice: Carry this: everyone has sorrow, including the people who post as if they don't. Talk soon.
